title: Depth-first search in NC
formal: Does there exist a logspace-uniform family of deterministic Boolean circuits of polynomial size and polylogarithmic depth that, on the adjacency matrix of every finite simple undirected graph, outputs a valid depth-first-search forest? The roots and the order of visiting neighbors may be chosen freely for each input.
why: DFS is a basic graph structure whose standard construction has a long chain of sequential choices. Resolving this question would determine whether randomness can always be removed from its efficient parallel construction while retaining polynomial total resources.

progress.text: Aggarwal and Anderson give a randomized NC algorithm for undirected DFS, as documented in the 2025 paper’s introduction. This permits randomness.
Ghaffari, Grunau and Qu give a randomized algorithm with \(\widetilde{O}\)\((m+n)\) work and \(\widetilde{O}\)\((\sqrt{n})\) depth; this addresses work efficiency with a larger depth bound.

Chauhan, Datta and Praveen prove deterministic parallel bounds for bounded-genus and undirected single-crossing-minor-free graphs, and a logspace bound for bounded treewidth. The general question remains open in their statement.

definitions: For \(n\ge 1\) the input is the \(n\times n\) symmetric zero-diagonal adjacency matrix of a graph G on \(V=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). The output is a parent array \(p\in \{0,\ldots ,n\}^{n}\), with 0 denoting a root. If \(p(v)\ne 0\), require \(\{v,p(v)\}\in E(G)\); repeatedly taking parents must reach 0 from every vertex. These parent edges define a rooted forest, and each connected component of G must be spanned by one of its trees. A vertex u is an ancestor of v if u lies on the tree path from v to its root. The forest is a DFS forest if, for every edge \(\{u,v\}\in E(G)\), one endpoint is an ancestor of the other. For undirected graphs this is exactly the class of forests produced by recursive depth-first search under some choices of roots and neighbor orders. Encode each parent entry in \(\lceil \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Each circuit \(C_{n}\) has \(n^{2}\) input bits and \(n\lceil \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil\) output bits, uses AND and OR gates with at most two inputs and NOT gates with one input, and has size at most \(O(n^{c})\) and depth at most \(O((\log _{2}(n+2))^{k})\), for fixed constants c,k independent of n and G. Logspace uniformity means that one deterministic Turing machine, given \(1^{n}\), writes the description of \(C_{n}\) while using \(O(\log (n+2))\) working space, excluding its read-only input and write-only output tapes. Correctness is required on every valid adjacency matrix; behavior on other bit strings is unrestricted. The empty graph has the empty output. No randomness or input-length-specific advice is supplied. NC here refers to computing a valid encoded output, rather than deciding a Boolean language.
answer_criterion: Construct one circuit family satisfying all the stated correctness, uniformity, size and depth requirements, or prove that no such family exists. The output may be any valid DFS forest. A randomized algorithm, a quasipolynomial-size circuit family, an algorithm only for a restricted graph class, or a lower bound for one prescribed traversal order does not settle this question.

context_blocks.text: Depth-first search explores an unvisited neighbor, completes the recursive exploration from that neighbor, and only then tries another neighbor of the current vertex. The resulting parent pointers form a spanning forest. The question asks whether that structure can always be assembled in a small number of parallel stages, even though the familiar sequential procedure follows one exploration at a time.

Being a spanning tree is not enough. In a triangle with vertices 1, 2 and 3, a tree rooted at 1 with children 2 and 3 fails: edge \(\{2,3\}\) joins different branches. The path with parent pointers \(p(1)=0, p(2)=1\) and \(p(3)=2\) is a valid DFS tree. The ancestor condition makes this distinction explicit without prescribing a traversal order.

The height of the output tree is not the running time being bounded. A path graph may require a DFS tree of height \(n- 1\), yet its n parent entries may be computed in parallel. Conversely, a sequential algorithm with linear running time need not have polylogarithmic parallel depth.

The freedom to choose a valid output matters. Reproducing the lexicographically first DFS order under fixed choices is P-complete according to the cited source. That hardness result does not exclude efficient parallel computation of a different valid DFS forest.

The general undirected problem has a randomized NC algorithm, and a deterministic parallel algorithm with quasipolynomially many processors is known. The latter exceeds the polynomial resource bound in this question. Deterministic NC algorithms are also known for several restricted graph families. The 2025 source still leaves general deterministic NC open.

There is a separate goal of keeping total work close to the input size. The 2023 algorithm obtains work \(\widetilde{O}\)\((m+n)\) and depth \(\widetilde{O}\)\((\sqrt{n})\), where m is the number of edges and \(\widetilde{O}\) suppresses factors polynomial in logarithms. Its depth bound is sublinear but does not establish the polylogarithmic depth required here.

Uniformity requires one small-space procedure to describe the circuits for every input length. The circuits cannot be unrelated choices supplied separately for each n. Both this requirement and the polynomial size bound belong to the target; merely showing that suitable circuits exist with larger resources leaves a different question.

sentences: A depth-first-search forest records the parent choices of recursive graph exploration.
For an undirected graph, it is a rooted spanning forest in which every graph edge joins a vertex to one of its ancestors.
The problem asks for a deterministic, uniformly specified parallel computation that constructs any such forest with polynomial resources and polylogarithmic depth.
Randomized NC algorithms and deterministic results for restricted graph classes are known, but those guarantees do not settle the general target.
A solution would show whether this basic search structure can always be built efficiently in parallel without random choices.
